blocks.es_reference: Unidad 2 · 2 Timoteo 2:2 · 100–313 d.C.

blocks.en: Apostolic Fathers, Persecutions, & Apologists
blocks.es_reference: Padres Apostólicos, Persecuciones, y Apologistas

blocks.en: "Commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also."
blocks.es_reference: «Encomiéndalas a hombres fieles que sean idóneos para enseñar también a otros».

blocks.en: Unit Scripture: "And the things that you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also." — 2 Timothy 2:2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: Escritura de la Unidad: «Y lo que has oído de mí entre muchos testigos, esto encarga a hombres fieles que sean idóneos para enseñar también a otros». — 2 Timoteo 2:2 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation: After the Apostles
blocks.es_reference: Orientación: Después de los apóstoles

blocks.en: When John died on Patmos around AD 100, the apostolic age was over. The men who had walked with Jesus were gone. The men who had laid the foundation were gone. The text they had left behind — what we call the New Testament — was now the church's only direct connection to its origins. And the church faced four questions all at once.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando Juan murió en Patmos alrededor del 100 d.C., la era apostólica había terminado. Los hombres que habían caminado con Jesús se habían ido. Los hombres que habían puesto el fundamento se habían ido. El texto que habían dejado atrás — lo que llamamos el Nuevo Testamento — era ahora la única conexión directa de la iglesia con sus orígenes. Y la iglesia enfrentó cuatro preguntas a la vez.

blocks.en: Who has authority now? The apostles had been the final word in any dispute. With them gone, where does authority sit? What exactly do we believe? The apostles had answered theological questions on the spot. With them gone, who answers the next one? How do we survive? The Roman Empire was tightening its grip, and a faith that refused to bow to Caesar was about to find out what Caesar did with such people. How do we sort the truth from the counterfeits? Heretics were already at the door, and some of them sounded a great deal like Christianity until you read the fine print.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Quién tiene autoridad ahora? Los apóstoles habían sido la palabra final en cualquier disputa. Con ellos idos, ¿dónde reside la autoridad? ¿Qué creemos exactamente? Los apóstoles habían respondido preguntas teológicas en el momento. Con ellos idos, ¿quién responde la siguiente? ¿Cómo sobrevivimos? El Imperio Romano estaba apretando su control, y una fe que se negaba a postrarse ante César estaba a punto de descubrir qué hacía César con tales personas. ¿Cómo distinguimos la verdad de las falsificaciones? Los herejes ya estaban a la puerta, y algunos de ellos sonaban muchísimo como cristianismo hasta que se leía la letra pequeña.

blocks.en: "Commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also."
blocks.es_reference: «Esto encarga a hombres fieles que sean idóneos para enseñar también a otros».

blocks.en: Unit 2 covers two hundred and thirteen years — from John's death around AD 100 to the Edict of Milan in 313 when the Emperor Constantine made Christianity legal at last. In that span the church will be tested by three forces: persecution, which tried to kill her; heresy, which tried to redefine her; and the slow, costly work of definition, in which she had to figure out what she actually believed before she could defend it. Three groups of men did the heavy lifting. The Apostolic Fathers sought to preserve and transmit the apostles' teaching to the generation that followed, when memory alone could have let it drift. The martyrs and confessors bought the church's continued existence with their lives. The Apologists defended the faith intellectually before a hostile pagan culture and forced the church to put her convictions into clear words.
blocks.es_reference: La Unidad 2 cubre doscientos trece años — desde la muerte de Juan alrededor del 100 d.C. hasta el Edicto de Milán en el 313 cuando el Emperador Constantino hizo legal el cristianismo por fin. En ese lapso la iglesia será probada por tres fuerzas: la persecución, que trató de matarla; la herejía, que trató de redefinirla; y la obra lenta y costosa de definición, en la cual tuvo que averiguar qué creía realmente antes de poder defenderlo. Tres grupos de hombres hicieron el trabajo pesado. Los Padres Apostólicos buscaron preservar y transmitir la enseñanza de los apóstoles a la generación que los siguió, cuando la memoria sola pudo haberla dejado desviarse. Los mártires y confesores compraron con sus vidas la existencia continuada de la iglesia. Los Apologistas defendieron la fe intelectualmente ante una cultura pagana hostil y obligaron a la iglesia a poner sus convicciones en palabras claras.

blocks.en: This is not a star unit on the four great centuries of preaching — the second century is too consumed with survival to produce a Chrysostom — but the men of this unit kept the apostolic pulpit alive. They preached as they could, where they could, until the church reached the freedom that would let the fourth century explode. Without them, there is no Augustine. Without Augustine, there is no Luther. Without Luther, there is no Spurgeon. Every later glory in this course rests on the obedience of men whose names most Christians have forgotten.
blocks.es_reference: Esta no es una unidad estrella en los cuatro grandes siglos de predicación — el segundo siglo está demasiado consumido por la supervivencia para producir un Crisóstomo — pero los hombres de esta unidad mantuvieron vivo el púlpito apostólico. Predicaron como pudieron, donde pudieron, hasta que la iglesia alcanzara la libertad que permitiría al cuarto siglo explotar. Sin ellos, no hay Agustín. Sin Agustín, no hay Lutero. Sin Lutero, no hay Spurgeon. Toda gloria posterior en este curso descansa sobre la obediencia de hombres cuyos nombres la mayoría de los cristianos han olvidado.

blocks.en: I. The Apostolic Fathers
blocks.es_reference: I. Los Padres Apostólicos

blocks.en: The Apostolic Fathers were Christian leaders of the late first and early second centuries who had either personally known the apostles or were directly influenced by men who had. Their writings form a bridge between the New Testament and the more developed theology of later centuries. They are not Scripture — the church has always recognized that — but they are the first commentary on Scripture by men who had stood close enough to its authors to know what they meant.
blocks.es_reference: Los Padres Apostólicos fueron líderes cristianos de finales del primer siglo y principios del segundo que habían conocido personalmente a los apóstoles o habían sido influenciados directamente por hombres que sí. Sus escritos forman un puente entre el Nuevo Testamento y la teología más desarrollada de siglos posteriores. No son Escritura — la iglesia siempre lo ha reconocido — pero son el primer comentario sobre la Escritura hecho por hombres que se habían parado lo suficientemente cerca de sus autores para saber lo que significaban.

blocks.en: Clement of Rome (c. AD 96)
blocks.es_reference: Clemente de Roma (c. 96 d.C.)

blocks.en: Clement was an elder of the church at Rome at the end of the first century. When the church at Corinth fell into a leadership dispute — the same Corinth Paul had written to forty years earlier with the same kinds of problems — Clement wrote them a letter we now call 1 Clement. It is the oldest Christian writing outside the New Testament. The letter pleads for humility, order, submission to elders, and the unity Christ prayed for in John 17. Clement quotes Old Testament examples, cites Pauline letters as authoritative, and writes in the calm pastoral voice of a man who learned his craft watching the apostles do it. The Corinthian church received the letter and kept it. They read it in worship for two more centuries. The first post-apostolic generation knew exactly what kind of writing it had inherited.
blocks.es_reference: Clemente fue un anciano de la iglesia en Roma al final del primer siglo. Cuando la iglesia de Corinto cayó en una disputa de liderazgo — la misma Corinto a la que Pablo había escrito cuarenta años antes con los mismos tipos de problemas — Clemente les escribió una carta que ahora llamamos 1 Clemente. Es el escrito cristiano más antiguo fuera del Nuevo Testamento. La carta suplica humildad, orden, sumisión a los ancianos, y la unidad por la cual Cristo oró en Juan 17. Clemente cita ejemplos del Antiguo Testamento, cita las cartas paulinas como autoritativas, y escribe en la voz pastoral calmada de un hombre que aprendió su oficio viendo a los apóstoles hacerlo. La iglesia corintia recibió la carta y la guardó. La leyeron en la adoración por dos siglos más. La primera generación post-apostólica sabía exactamente qué tipo de escrito había heredado.

blocks.en: Ignatius of Antioch (martyred c. AD 110)
blocks.es_reference: Ignacio de Antioquía (martirizado c. 110 d.C.)

blocks.en: Ignatius was bishop of Antioch — the same Antioch where the disciples had first been called Christians, the same Antioch from which Paul had launched his missionary journeys. About AD 110 he was arrested and sent to Rome under armed escort to die in the arena. Along the way, in chains, he wrote seven letters to the churches he passed near. The letters reveal a man eager for martyrdom: "Let me be food for the wild beasts, through whom I can attain to God," he wrote to the Romans, asking them not to interfere with his death. He insisted on the full reality of Christ's incarnation against early Docetic teachers who claimed Jesus only seemed to have a body. He insisted on the authority of bishops as a hedge against confusion. And he died in Rome, somewhere around AD 110, exactly as he had asked.
blocks.es_reference: Ignacio fue obispo de Antioquía — la misma Antioquía donde a los discípulos se les había llamado cristianos por primera vez, la misma Antioquía desde la cual Pablo había lanzado sus viajes misioneros. Alrededor del 110 d.C. fue arrestado y enviado a Roma bajo escolta armada para morir en la arena. En el camino, en cadenas, escribió siete cartas a las iglesias por las que pasó cerca. Las cartas revelan a un hombre ansioso por el martirio: «Déjenme ser comida para las bestias salvajes, por las cuales puedo alcanzar a Dios», escribió a los romanos, pidiéndoles que no interfirieran con su muerte. Insistió en la plena realidad de la encarnación de Cristo contra maestros docéticos tempranos que afirmaban que Jesús solo parecía tener un cuerpo. Insistió en la autoridad de los obispos como un seto contra la confusión. Y murió en Roma, alrededor del 110 d.C., exactamente como había pedido.

blocks.en: Polycarp of Smyrna (martyred c. AD 155)
blocks.es_reference: Policarpo de Esmirna (martirizado c. 155 d.C.)

blocks.en: Polycarp was a disciple of the apostle John. Let that sink in. The man who wrote 1 John, the man who leaned against Jesus's chest at the Last Supper — that man taught Polycarp. Polycarp grew up to become the bishop of Smyrna, modern-day Izmir on the western coast of Turkey, and he served his church faithfully into his eighties. About AD 155, when Polycarp was eighty-six years old, the Roman authorities came for him. They offered him a way out: a pinch of incense to Caesar's image, a quick denial of Christ, and he could go home and die in his bed.
blocks.es_reference: Policarpo fue discípulo del apóstol Juan. Que eso se asiente. El hombre que escribió 1 Juan, el hombre que se reclinó sobre el pecho de Jesús en la Última Cena — ese hombre enseñó a Policarpo. Policarpo creció para convertirse en el obispo de Esmirna, la moderna Izmir en la costa occidental de Turquía, y sirvió fielmente a su iglesia hasta sus ochenta. Alrededor del 155 d.C., cuando Policarpo tenía ochenta y seis años, las autoridades romanas vinieron por él. Le ofrecieron una salida: una pizca de incienso a la imagen de César, una negación rápida de Cristo, y podría irse a casa y morir en su cama.

blocks.en: Polycarp refused. The proconsul pressed him: think of his age, think of his dignity, just curse Christ and live. Polycarp answered with words that have been remembered for nineteen centuries: "Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He has done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" They burned him at the stake, and when the fire seemed to refuse to touch him, a soldier finished the job with a sword. The eyewitness account, called the Martyrdom of Polycarp, is the first detailed Christian martyrdom narrative we possess outside the New Testament. It became a model for what Christian dying looks like when it is done well.
blocks.es_reference: Policarpo se negó. El procónsul presionó: piense en su edad, piense en su dignidad, solo maldiga a Cristo y viva. Policarpo respondió con palabras que se han recordado por diecinueve siglos: «Ochenta y seis años le he servido, y ningún mal me ha hecho. ¿Cómo entonces puedo blasfemar a mi Rey que me salvó?» Lo quemaron en la hoguera, y cuando el fuego pareció rehusarse a tocarlo, un soldado terminó el trabajo con una espada. El relato de testigos oculares, llamado El Martirio de Policarpo, es la primera narrativa detallada de un martirio cristiano que poseemos fuera del Nuevo Testamento. Se convirtió en un modelo de cómo se ve el morir cristiano cuando se hace bien.

blocks.en: The church's chain of teaching has never been broken — that from Christ to the apostles, from the apostles to men like Polycarp, from Polycarp to his student Irenaeus, from Irenaeus down through every generation since, there has always been a living link. When you stand in the line of Christian teachers today, that is the line you are standing in. Polycarp is one of the bolts that holds it together.
blocks.es_reference: La cadena de enseñanza de la iglesia nunca se ha roto — que de Cristo a los apóstoles, de los apóstoles a hombres como Policarpo, de Policarpo a su discípulo Ireneo, de Ireneo hacia abajo por cada generación desde entonces, siempre ha habido un eslabón vivo. Cuando usted se para hoy en la línea de los maestros cristianos, esa es la línea en la que está parado. Policarpo es uno de los pernos que la mantiene unida.

blocks.en: Other writings
blocks.es_reference: Otros escritos

blocks.en: Several other early documents fill out the period: the Didache (or "Teaching of the Twelve Apostles"), a brief manual of Christian instruction on baptism, the Lord's Supper, prayer, and the testing of traveling teachers; the Epistle of Barnabas, an exposition of Old Testament types fulfilled in Christ; and the Shepherd of Hermas, a long visionary work on repentance. These books were widely read, sometimes nearly canonical in some regions, but the church in time recognized that they belonged in a different category from the apostolic writings. The Apostolic Fathers were faithful echoes. The apostles themselves were the original voice.
blocks.es_reference: Varios otros documentos tempranos completan el período: la Didaché (o «Enseñanza de los Doce Apóstoles»), un breve manual de instrucción cristiana sobre el bautismo, la Cena del Señor, la oración, y la prueba de los maestros itinerantes; la Epístola de Bernabé, una exposición de tipos del Antiguo Testamento cumplidos en Cristo; y el Pastor de Hermas, una larga obra visionaria sobre el arrepentimiento. Estos libros fueron ampliamente leídos, a veces casi canónicos en algunas regiones, pero la iglesia con el tiempo reconoció que pertenecían a una categoría diferente de los escritos apostólicos. Los Padres Apostólicos fueron ecos fieles. Los apóstoles mismos fueron la voz original.

blocks.en: II. Persecution Under Rome
blocks.es_reference: II. Persecución bajo Roma

blocks.en: Why did Rome hate the Christians? Rome had absorbed every conquered religion into its pantheon for five hundred years; one more god, one more cult, was supposed to be no problem. The Christians were a problem. Four reasons made them so.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Por qué odiaba Roma a los cristianos? Roma había absorbido cada religión conquistada en su panteón por quinientos años; un dios más, un culto más, se suponía que no era problema. Los cristianos eran un problema. Cuatro razones los hicieron así.

blocks.en: First, Christians refused to participate in emperor worship and pagan sacrifices. Every public event in the Roman world — civic festivals, military oaths, business associations, even guild meetings — included a small sacrifice to the gods or a pinch of incense to the emperor. Christians would not. They were called atheists, not because they denied God, but because they denied the gods — every god the empire recognized. Second, rumors spread about what Christians did at their love feasts. They greeted each other with a holy kiss, ate together, and called each other "brother" and "sister." Roman gossip turned that into incest. Third, the Lord's Supper involved language about eating the body and drinking the blood of Christ. Roman gossip turned that into cannibalism. Fourth, when fire or plague or military defeat struck the empire, someone had to be blamed. The old gods seemed angry. Why? Because the Christians were not honoring them. Burn the Christians, and maybe the gods will calm down.
blocks.es_reference: Primera, los cristianos rehusaban participar en la adoración al emperador y los sacrificios paganos. Cada evento público en el mundo romano — festivales cívicos, juramentos militares, asociaciones de negocios, incluso reuniones de gremios — incluía un pequeño sacrificio a los dioses o una pizca de incienso al emperador. Los cristianos no lo hacían. Se les llamaba ateos, no porque negaran a Dios, sino porque negaban a los dioses — cada dios que el imperio reconocía. Segunda, los rumores se extendieron sobre lo que los cristianos hacían en sus ágapes o fiestas de amor. Se saludaban con un beso santo, comían juntos, y se llamaban «hermano» y «hermana». El chisme romano convirtió eso en incesto. Tercera, la Cena del Señor involucraba lenguaje sobre comer el cuerpo y beber la sangre de Cristo. El chisme romano convirtió eso en canibalismo. Cuarta, cuando el fuego, la plaga, o la derrota militar golpeaban al imperio, alguien tenía que ser culpado. Los antiguos dioses parecían enojados. ¿Por qué? Porque los cristianos no los honraban. Quemen a los cristianos, y quizás los dioses se calmarán.

blocks.en: The persecution arc ran for two and a half centuries. Some emperors were ferocious; others looked the other way. The big names track the worst of it.
blocks.es_reference: El arco de persecución se extendió por dos siglos y medio. Algunos emperadores fueron feroces; otros miraron para otro lado. Los nombres grandes rastrean lo peor.

blocks.en: Nero (AD 64)
blocks.es_reference: Nerón (64 d.C.)

blocks.en: Rome burned for six days in July of AD 64. The popular blame fell on Nero himself, who needed a scapegoat fast. He found one in the Christians. The historian Tacitus, no friend of Christianity, recorded that Nero had Christians wrapped in animal skins and torn apart by dogs, nailed to crosses, or set on fire to light his garden parties at night. Peter and Paul almost certainly died in this Neronian persecution, Peter crucified (by tradition upside down), Paul beheaded as a Roman citizen.
blocks.es_reference: Roma ardió por seis días en julio del 64 d.C. La culpa popular cayó sobre el mismo Nerón, que necesitaba un chivo expiatorio rápido. Encontró uno en los cristianos. El historiador Tácito, no amigo del cristianismo, registró que Nerón hizo envolver a cristianos en pieles de animales y desgarrar por perros, clavar en cruces, o prenderles fuego para iluminar sus fiestas de jardín por la noche. Pedro y Pablo casi con certeza murieron en esta persecución neroniana, Pedro crucificado (por tradición al revés), Pablo decapitado como ciudadano romano.

blocks.en: Trajan (c. AD 112)
blocks.es_reference: Trajano (c. 112 d.C.)

blocks.en: The governor Pliny the Younger, stationed in what is now northern Turkey, wrote to the Emperor Trajan asking what to do about the swelling Christian population. Trajan replied with a famous line: do not seek them out, but if they are denounced and refuse to recant, punish them. This became Roman policy for nearly a century. It made Christianity unsafe but not actively hunted.
blocks.es_reference: El gobernador Plinio el Joven, estacionado en lo que ahora es el norte de Turquía, escribió al Emperador Trajano preguntando qué hacer con la creciente población cristiana. Trajano respondió con una línea famosa: no los busquen, pero si son denunciados y rehúsan retractarse, castíguenlos. Esto se convirtió en política romana por casi un siglo. Hizo que el cristianismo fuera inseguro pero no activamente cazado.

blocks.en: Marcus Aurelius (161–180)
blocks.es_reference: Marco Aurelio (161–180)

blocks.en: The philosopher-emperor permitted local outbreaks of persecution. Justin Martyr was executed in Rome around 165. The brutal persecution at Lyons in 177 produced the slave girl Blandina, who was scourged, thrown to wild beasts, roasted on a hot iron chair, and finally killed in a net before a bull — and she never recanted.
blocks.es_reference: El emperador-filósofo permitió brotes locales de persecución. Justino Mártir fue ejecutado en Roma alrededor del 165. La brutal persecución en Lyon en el 177 produjo a la esclava Blandina, que fue azotada, arrojada a las bestias salvajes, asada en una silla de hierro caliente, y finalmente muerta en una red ante un toro — y nunca se retractó.

blocks.en: Decius (250–251)

Decius issued the first empire-wide demand: every citizen must offer sacrifice to the Roman gods and obtain a certificate (a libellus) proving compliance. The persecution was administrative, paperwork-driven, and devastating. The libellus system left a paper trail that haunted the church for years.
blocks.es_reference: Decio emitió la primera demanda a escala imperial: cada ciudadano debía ofrecer sacrificio a los dioses romanos y obtener un certificado (un libellus) que probara el cumplimiento. La persecución era administrativa, impulsada por papeleo, y devastadora. El sistema de libelli dejó un rastro de papel que atormentó a la iglesia por años.

blocks.en: Diocletian (303–311)
blocks.es_reference: Diocleciano (303–311)

blocks.en: The "Great Persecution," the most severe empire-wide attack on Christians the church ever faced. Diocletian ordered Scriptures burned, churches destroyed, clergy imprisoned, and the laity forced to sacrifice. It went on for eight years and ended only when the emperor's successors began to grasp that they could not kill the church faster than it grew.
blocks.es_reference: La «Gran Persecución», el ataque a escala imperial más severo contra los cristianos que la iglesia jamás enfrentó. Diocleciano ordenó que se quemaran las Escrituras, se destruyeran las iglesias, se encarcelaran al clero, y se obligara al laicado a sacrificar. Se prolongó por ocho años y terminó solo cuando los sucesores del emperador comenzaron a captar que no podían matar a la iglesia más rápido de lo que crecía.

blocks.en: Why did persecution fail? The North African lawyer Tertullian, writing about AD 200, gave the most famous answer in church history: the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church. Every public execution was a free advertisement. Pagan crowds went to the arena to watch Christians die well, and some of them went home Christians. Persecution scattered the church but did not extinguish it. Persecution refined the church but did not corrupt it. Persecution killed individual Christians but multiplied Christianity.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Por qué falló la persecución? El abogado norteafricano Tertuliano, escribiendo alrededor del 200 d.C., dio la respuesta más famosa en la historia de la iglesia: la sangre de los mártires es la semilla de la iglesia. Cada ejecución pública era un anuncio gratis. Las multitudes paganas iban a la arena para ver a los cristianos morir bien, y algunas de ellas se iban a casa cristianas. La persecución dispersó a la iglesia pero no la extinguió. La persecución refinó a la iglesia pero no la corrompió. La persecución mató a cristianos individuales pero multiplicó al cristianismo.

blocks.en: That is a pattern worth remembering when comfort returns. The church is most vulnerable not in persecution but in prosperity. The church under Nero grew. The church under Constantine, when imperial favor would arrive in 313, would face a different and subtler test — the test of being liked. We will watch that test in Unit 3.
blocks.es_reference: Ese es un patrón que vale la pena recordar cuando regresa la comodidad. La iglesia es más vulnerable no en la persecución sino en la prosperidad. La iglesia bajo Nerón creció. La iglesia bajo Constantino, cuando el favor imperial llegaría en el 313, enfrentaría una prueba diferente y más sutil — la prueba de ser apreciada. Veremos esa prueba en la Unidad 3.

blocks.en: III. The Great Heresies
blocks.es_reference: III. Las grandes herejías

blocks.en: The word heresy in Greek means a choice — the choice to pick out a piece of the truth and exalt it above the whole. In Christian usage, heresy is the formal denial of a core doctrine of the faith. Heresy is not honest disagreement on minor matters. It is the rejection or fundamental distortion of something the church has always believed.
blocks.es_reference: La palabra herejía en griego significa una elección — la elección de tomar una pieza de la verdad y exaltarla por encima del todo. En el uso cristiano, la herejía es la negación formal de una doctrina central de la fe. La herejía no es desacuerdo honesto en asuntos menores. Es el rechazo o la distorsión fundamental de algo que la iglesia siempre ha creído.

blocks.en: Why did heresies erupt in the second century? Because the timing was perfect for them. The apostles were dead, so first-hand correction was impossible. The New Testament canon had not yet been formally collected, so settling a dispute by saying "let me read you what Paul said" was harder than it sounds. Theology was still being articulated, so any clever teacher with a new framework could find an audience. Three heresies dominated the period, and all three are still with us in modern dress.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Por qué irrumpieron las herejías en el segundo siglo? Porque el momento era perfecto para ellas. Los apóstoles estaban muertos, así que la corrección de primera mano era imposible. El canon del Nuevo Testamento aún no había sido recopilado formalmente, así que resolver una disputa diciendo «déjame leerte lo que dijo Pablo» era más difícil de lo que suena. La teología aún se estaba articulando, así que cualquier maestro listo con un marco nuevo podía encontrar audiencia. Tres herejías dominaron el período, y las tres siguen con nosotros vestidas de moderno.

blocks.en: Gnosticism
blocks.es_reference: Gnosticismo

blocks.en: The most diffuse and dangerous heresy of the era. Gnosticism was less a single movement than a family of movements that shared a worldview. Reality, the Gnostics taught, is divided sharply between spirit (good) and matter (evil). The God of the Old Testament, who created this evil material world, must therefore be a lower, flawed deity — the Gnostics called him the Demiurge. The true high God is far above him, unknowable to ordinary minds. Salvation is escape from matter into pure spirit, and it is achieved through secret knowledge — in Greek, gnosis — which the Gnostic teachers claimed to possess and dispense to initiates.
blocks.es_reference: La herejía más difusa y peligrosa de la era. El gnosticismo era menos un solo movimiento que una familia de movimientos que compartían una cosmovisión. La realidad, enseñaban los gnósticos, está dividida marcadamente entre espíritu (bueno) y materia (mala). El Dios del Antiguo Testamento, que creó este mundo material malvado, debe por tanto ser una deidad inferior y defectuosa — los gnósticos lo llamaban el Demiurgo. El verdadero Dios alto está muy por encima de él, incognoscible para mentes ordinarias. La salvación es escape de la materia al espíritu puro, y se logra mediante conocimiento secreto — en griego, gnosis — que los maestros gnósticos pretendían poseer y dispensar a los iniciados.

blocks.en: Christ, in Gnostic teaching, could not have actually taken on a real human body, because matter is evil. So most Gnostics were Docetists: they taught that Christ only seemed to have a body, that He was a phantom or projection. The cross, in this scheme, was either an illusion or a release. The bodily resurrection was unthinkable. Salvation was for the soul alone.
blocks.es_reference: Cristo, en la enseñanza gnóstica, no podría haber tomado realmente un cuerpo humano real, porque la materia es mala. Así que la mayoría de los gnósticos eran docetistas: enseñaban que Cristo solo parecía tener un cuerpo, que era un fantasma o una proyección. La cruz, en este esquema, era una ilusión o una liberación. La resurrección corporal era impensable. La salvación era solo para el alma.

blocks.en: Read Colossians 2 carefully and you can already see Paul wrestling with proto-Gnostic teachers. Read 1 John and you find John insisting that "Jesus Christ has come in the flesh" — against people who said He had not. Gnosticism attacked three pillars at once: the goodness of creation, the reality of the incarnation, and the bodily resurrection. The orthodox response, hammered out by Irenaeus and others in this very period, was that God created matter and called it good, that the Word truly became flesh, and that the Christ who died will bodily raise His people on the last day.
blocks.es_reference: Lea Colosenses 2 cuidadosamente y ya puede ver a Pablo luchando con maestros proto-gnósticos. Lea 1 Juan y encuentra a Juan insistiendo en que «Jesucristo ha venido en carne» — contra personas que decían que no. El gnosticismo atacaba tres pilares a la vez: la bondad de la creación, la realidad de la encarnación, y la resurrección corporal. La respuesta ortodoxa, forjada por Ireneo y otros en este mismo período, fue que Dios creó la materia y la llamó buena, que el Verbo verdaderamente se hizo carne, y que el Cristo que murió levantará corporalmente a su pueblo en el último día.

blocks.en: Marcionism
blocks.es_reference: Marcionismo

blocks.en: Marcion of Sinope, a wealthy shipowner who came to Rome about AD 140, was offended by the harsher passages of the Old Testament and by the contrast he thought he saw between the OT God of judgment and the NT God of grace. So Marcion solved the problem by amputation. He rejected the entire Old Testament. He rejected most of the New Testament. He kept an edited version of Luke's Gospel and ten of Paul's letters with the Jewish elements scrubbed out, and he announced that this was the true Christian canon. The God of Jesus, said Marcion, was not the God of Moses. The two were different beings. The Old Testament could be discarded.
blocks.es_reference: Marción de Sínope, un rico armador que llegó a Roma alrededor del 140 d.C., se ofendió por los pasajes más duros del Antiguo Testamento y por el contraste que creyó ver entre el Dios del juicio del AT y el Dios de gracia del NT. Así que Marción resolvió el problema por amputación. Rechazó el Antiguo Testamento entero. Rechazó la mayoría del Nuevo Testamento. Conservó una versión editada del Evangelio de Lucas y diez de las cartas de Pablo con los elementos judíos eliminados, y anunció que este era el verdadero canon cristiano. El Dios de Jesús, dijo Marción, no era el Dios de Moisés. Los dos eran seres diferentes. El Antiguo Testamento podía ser descartado.

blocks.en: The church excommunicated Marcion in 144 and never looked back. But Marcion did the church one accidental favor: by publishing his amputated canon, he forced the orthodox church to start asking, "What is our canon?" By the end of the second century, leaders were circulating lists of accepted books. The Muratorian Fragment, dated about 170 AD, lists most of the books we now call the New Testament. Marcion's heresy did not damage the canon. Marcion's heresy accelerated the canon.
blocks.es_reference: La iglesia excomulgó a Marción en el 144 y nunca volvió la vista atrás. Pero Marción le hizo a la iglesia un favor accidental: al publicar su canon amputado, obligó a la iglesia ortodoxa a comenzar a preguntar: «¿Cuál es nuestro canon?» Para finales del segundo siglo, los líderes circulaban listas de libros aceptados. El Fragmento Muratoriano, fechado alrededor del 170 d.C., enumera la mayoría de los libros que ahora llamamos el Nuevo Testamento. La herejía de Marción no dañó al canon. La herejía de Marción aceleró el canon.

blocks.en: Montanism
blocks.es_reference: Montanismo

blocks.en: About AD 170, in Phrygia, a recent convert named Montanus began prophesying in ecstatic trances. Two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, joined him with prophecies of their own. They called their movement the New Prophecy. Their claim was that the age of apostolic teaching was passing and a new outpouring of the Spirit was coming through them. They demanded extreme asceticism, forbade remarriage after the death of a spouse, and announced the imminent return of Christ to a town in Phrygia called Pepuza, where the New Jerusalem would descend.
blocks.es_reference: Alrededor del 170 d.C., en Frigia, un converso reciente llamado Montano comenzó a profetizar en trances extáticos. Dos mujeres, Priscila y Maximila, se le unieron con sus propias profecías. Llamaron a su movimiento la Nueva Profecía. Su afirmación era que la era de la enseñanza apostólica estaba pasando y un nuevo derramamiento del Espíritu venía a través de ellos. Demandaban un ascetismo extremo, prohibían el segundo matrimonio tras la muerte del cónyuge, y anunciaban el inminente regreso de Cristo a un pueblo de Frigia llamado Pepuza, donde la Nueva Jerusalén descendería.

blocks.en: The Montanists were not heretics in the Gnostic sense. Their doctrine was largely orthodox. The threat they posed was different: they claimed that the Spirit's revelation continued at full apostolic intensity through their own prophets, effectively superseding the New Testament that was just then being collected. The orthodox response was that the apostolic deposit is closed. The Spirit still teaches, still convicts, still empowers, but He does not contradict or supplement the apostles. The line had to be drawn, and it was.
blocks.es_reference: Los montanistas no eran herejes en el sentido gnóstico. Su doctrina era ampliamente ortodoxa. La amenaza que representaban era diferente: afirmaban que la revelación del Espíritu continuaba con plena intensidad apostólica a través de sus propios profetas, suplantando efectivamente al Nuevo Testamento que justo entonces se estaba recopilando. La respuesta ortodoxa fue que el depósito apostólico está cerrado. El Espíritu aún enseña, aún convence, aún empodera, pero no contradice ni suplementa a los apóstoles. La línea tenía que trazarse, y se trazó.

blocks.en: One footnote on Montanism that will matter later: when Priscilla and Maximilla were prominent female prophets in a heretical movement, the orthodox church recoiled from women in similar visible roles. By the late second century, the male leadership pattern that had not been universal in the first century became increasingly the norm. The first-century church wove women's gifts into its life freely. The post-Montanist church grew cautious. That is one of the costs of heresy that does not get talked about often.
blocks.es_reference: Una nota al pie sobre el montanismo que importará después: cuando Priscila y Maximila eran profetisas femeninas prominentes en un movimiento herético, la iglesia ortodoxa retrocedió de las mujeres en roles visibles similares. Para finales del segundo siglo, el patrón de liderazgo masculino que no había sido universal en el primer siglo se volvió cada vez más la norma. La iglesia del primer siglo entretejió libremente los dones de las mujeres en su vida. La iglesia post-montanista se volvió cautelosa. Ese es uno de los costos de la herejía de los que no se habla a menudo.

blocks.en: IV. The Apologists
blocks.es_reference: IV. Los Apologistas

blocks.en: While the Apostolic Fathers preserved apostolic teaching for the church, the Apologists defended the faith to the world. They were educated Christians, often classically trained in Greek philosophy and Roman rhetoric, who argued the case for Christianity before pagan emperors, philosophers, and intellectual elites. Three of them deserve special attention.
blocks.es_reference: Mientras los Padres Apostólicos preservaron la enseñanza apostólica para la iglesia, los Apologistas defendieron la fe ante el mundo. Eran cristianos educados, a menudo entrenados clásicamente en filosofía griega y retórica romana, que argumentaron el caso del cristianismo ante emperadores paganos, filósofos, y élites intelectuales. Tres de ellos merecen atención especial.

blocks.en: Justin Martyr (c. 100–165)
blocks.es_reference: Justino Mártir (c. 100–165)

blocks.en: Justin was a Greek philosopher who tried Stoicism, Platonism, and Pythagoreanism without finding peace, until an old man on a beach pointed him to the Hebrew prophets. Justin became a Christian and continued to wear the philosopher's cloak as a Christian, signaling that Christianity was the true philosophy he had been seeking all along. His First Apology, addressed to the Emperor Antoninus Pius around AD 155, defended Christians against the popular slanders of incest and cannibalism by simply describing what Christians actually did at worship: they read the Scriptures, the elder explained them, they shared bread and wine, they cared for the poor. His Dialogue with Trypho argued from the Old Testament that Jesus is the promised Messiah. Justin opened a Christian school in Rome. He was beheaded around AD 165 along with several of his students. He had earned his second name.
blocks.es_reference: Justino era un filósofo griego que probó el estoicismo, el platonismo, y el pitagorismo sin encontrar paz, hasta que un anciano en una playa lo dirigió a los profetas hebreos. Justino se hizo cristiano y continuó vistiendo el manto del filósofo como cristiano, señalando que el cristianismo era la verdadera filosofía que había estado buscando todo el tiempo. Su Primera Apología, dirigida al Emperador Antonino Pío alrededor del 155 d.C., defendió a los cristianos contra las calumnias populares de incesto y canibalismo describiendo simplemente lo que los cristianos realmente hacían en la adoración: leían las Escrituras, el anciano las explicaba, compartían el pan y el vino, cuidaban a los pobres. Su Diálogo con Trifón argumentó desde el Antiguo Testamento que Jesús es el Mesías prometido. Justino abrió una escuela cristiana en Roma. Fue decapitado alrededor del 165 d.C. junto con varios de sus estudiantes. Se había ganado su segundo nombre.

blocks.en: Tertullian (c. 160–220)
blocks.es_reference: Tertuliano (c. 160–220)

blocks.en: Tertullian was a North African lawyer from Carthage who converted to Christianity in his thirties and brought his lawyer's pen with him. He wrote in Latin (Justin had written in Greek) and gave Western theology much of its early vocabulary. The word Trinity (trinitas) is his coinage. The phrase three persons in one substance is his formula. He wrote against Marcion in five massive volumes. He wrote against the gnostic Hermogenes. He wrote against the practice of soldiering for pagan armies. He wrote against women's elaborate dress and against Christians attending the games. His pen was sharp; his arguments were sharper. And it is from Tertullian that we get the great line about the church's growth: "The blood of the Christians is seed." Twenty centuries of preaching have paraphrased that sentence and never improved it.
blocks.es_reference: Tertuliano fue un abogado norteafricano de Cartago que se convirtió al cristianismo en sus treinta años y trajo consigo su pluma de abogado. Escribió en latín (Justino había escrito en griego) y le dio a la teología occidental mucho de su vocabulario temprano. La palabra Trinidad (trinitas) es su acuñación. La frase tres personas en una sustancia es su fórmula. Escribió contra Marción en cinco volúmenes masivos. Escribió contra el gnóstico Hermógenes. Escribió contra la práctica de servir como soldado para ejércitos paganos. Escribió contra el vestido elaborado de las mujeres y contra los cristianos que asistían a los juegos. Su pluma era afilada; sus argumentos eran más afilados. Y es de Tertuliano que obtenemos la gran línea sobre el crecimiento de la iglesia: «La sangre de los cristianos es semilla». Veinte siglos de predicación han parafraseado esa frase y nunca la han mejorado.

blocks.en: Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202)
blocks.es_reference: Ireneo de Lyon (c. 130–202)

blocks.en: Irenaeus is the man who closes the loop. He was born in Smyrna, where he heard Polycarp preach as a boy. Polycarp had heard the apostle John. Irenaeus, then, was just two handshakes away from Christ Himself. He became bishop of Lyons in southern Gaul, where he served the small Christian community there. About AD 180 he wrote his great five-book work Against Heresies, an exhaustive refutation of Gnosticism that summarized every Gnostic system he could find and then dismantled it from Scripture and from the rule of faith — the basic summary of Christian belief that every church everywhere had received from the apostles. Irenaeus's argument went like this: the Gnostics claim secret tradition; we have public tradition. The Gnostics claim secret writings; we have the public Scriptures. The Gnostics cannot trace their teachers back to the apostles; we can. Look at the chain. Polycarp taught me. John taught Polycarp. Christ taught John. Where, exactly, do you appear in that line, Mr. Gnostic?
blocks.es_reference: Ireneo es el hombre que cierra el círculo. Nació en Esmirna, donde de niño escuchó a Policarpo predicar. Policarpo había escuchado al apóstol Juan. Ireneo, entonces, estaba solo a dos apretones de manos del mismo Cristo. Se convirtió en obispo de Lyon en el sur de la Galia, donde sirvió a la pequeña comunidad cristiana allí. Alrededor del 180 d.C. escribió su gran obra de cinco libros Contra las Herejías, una refutación exhaustiva del gnosticismo que resumió cada sistema gnóstico que pudo encontrar y luego lo desmanteló desde la Escritura y desde la regla de fe — el resumen básico de la creencia cristiana que cada iglesia en todas partes había recibido de los apóstoles. El argumento de Ireneo iba así: los gnósticos afirman tradición secreta; nosotros tenemos tradición pública. Los gnósticos afirman escritos secretos; nosotros tenemos las Escrituras públicas. Los gnósticos no pueden rastrear a sus maestros hasta los apóstoles; nosotros sí. Mire la cadena. Policarpo me enseñó. Juan le enseñó a Policarpo. Cristo le enseñó a Juan. ¿Dónde, exactamente, aparece usted en esa línea, señor gnóstico?

blocks.en: That argument from apostolic succession — the idea that legitimate Christian teaching travels in an unbroken chain from the apostles to the present — was the church's most powerful weapon against gnosticism. The chain mattered because the message mattered. A teaching disconnected from the apostolic deposit had no claim on the church.
blocks.es_reference: Ese argumento desde la sucesión apostólica — la idea de que la enseñanza cristiana legítima viaja en una cadena ininterrumpida desde los apóstoles hasta el presente — fue el arma más poderosa de la iglesia contra el gnosticismo. La cadena importaba porque el mensaje importaba. Una enseñanza desconectada del depósito apostólico no tenía pretensión sobre la iglesia.

blocks.en: V. Confessors, the Lapsi, and the Canon
blocks.es_reference: V. Confesores, los lapsi, y el canon

blocks.en: The Decian persecution of 250–251 created a moral crisis the church had not faced before. The persecution was administrative, not random. Every citizen had to obtain a libellus — a certificate of sacrifice — from a Roman magistrate. When the persecution ended after about eighteen months, the church looked around and discovered that her members had taken four very different paths.
blocks.es_reference: La persecución de Decio del 250–251 creó una crisis moral que la iglesia no había enfrentado antes. La persecución era administrativa, no aleatoria. Cada ciudadano tenía que obtener un libellus — un certificado de sacrificio — de un magistrado romano. Cuando la persecución terminó después de unos dieciocho meses, la iglesia miró alrededor y descubrió que sus miembros habían tomado cuatro caminos muy diferentes.

blocks.en: The martyrs had refused the libellus and died for it. The confessors had refused the libellus, been tortured, and survived. They became living relics of the church's faithfulness, revered for the rest of their lives. The fugitives had fled the empire to wait out the storm. And then there were the lapsi — the lapsed — who had given in. They split into subgroups. The sacrificati had actually offered the sacrifice. The thurificati had burned the incense. The libellatici had bribed officials to issue them a certificate without performing the ritual. Some had sent slaves to sacrifice on their behalf. Some had clergy sign for them.
blocks.es_reference: Los mártires habían rechazado el libellus y muerto por ello. Los confesores habían rechazado el libellus, sido torturados, y sobrevivido. Se convirtieron en reliquias vivientes de la fidelidad de la iglesia, reverenciados por el resto de sus vidas. Los fugitivos habían huido del imperio para esperar la tormenta. Y luego estaban los lapsi — los caídos — que habían cedido. Se dividieron en subgrupos. Los sacrificati habían ofrecido realmente el sacrificio. Los thurificati habían quemado el incienso. Los libellatici habían sobornado a oficiales para que les emitieran un certificado sin realizar el ritual. Algunos habían enviado esclavos a sacrificar por ellos. Algunos hicieron que el clero firmara por ellos.

blocks.en: When the persecution ended, the lapsi began coming back to church and asking to be readmitted. The question split the church. The strict party said no — you denied Christ before men, He will deny you before His Father. The lenient party said yes — the church is a hospital, not a museum, and the lapsi need help. The middle party, led by Cyprian of Carthage, said yes with discipline: a period of public penance, then restoration. Cyprian's solution mostly held. The Donatists in the next century would reopen the wound (we will meet them in Unit 3), but the church had learned a hard lesson: persecution does not just produce martyrs. Persecution produces all four groups, and a wise church plans for that.
blocks.es_reference: Cuando la persecución terminó, los lapsi comenzaron a regresar a la iglesia y pedir ser readmitidos. La cuestión dividió a la iglesia. El partido estricto dijo no — usted negó a Cristo ante los hombres, Él lo negará ante Su Padre. El partido indulgente dijo sí — la iglesia es un hospital, no un museo, y los lapsi necesitan ayuda. El partido medio, liderado por Cipriano de Cartago, dijo sí con disciplina: un período de penitencia pública, luego restauración. La solución de Cipriano se mantuvo en general. Los donatistas del siglo siguiente reabrirían la herida (los conoceremos en la Unidad 3), pero la iglesia había aprendido una lección dura: la persecución no produce solo mártires. La persecución produce los cuatro grupos, y una iglesia sabia se prepara para eso.

blocks.en: Through this same period the New Testament canon was taking final shape. Marcion's heretical canon of 144 had forced the question. By about 170 the Muratorian Fragment listed most of the books we now have. By 200 the four Gospels, Acts, the thirteen Pauline letters, 1 Peter, and 1 John were universally accepted. A handful of books — Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, 2 and 3 John, Jude, Revelation — remained debated in some regions until the fourth century. The principle behind canonization was apostolic origin: a book was Scripture if it was written by an apostle or by someone working under direct apostolic authority, and if the church everywhere had received it. The church did not create the canon. The church recognized the canon. By the time Athanasius would publish his famous Festal Letter of 367 listing the full twenty-seven New Testament books, he was largely confirming what most Christians already knew.
blocks.es_reference: A través de este mismo período el canon del Nuevo Testamento estaba tomando forma final. El canon herético de Marción del 144 había forzado la pregunta. Para alrededor del 170 el Fragmento Muratoriano enumeraba la mayoría de los libros que ahora tenemos. Para el 200 los cuatro Evangelios, Hechos, las trece cartas paulinas, 1 Pedro, y 1 Juan eran universalmente aceptados. Un puñado de libros — Hebreos, Santiago, 2 Pedro, 2 y 3 Juan, Judas, Apocalipsis — permaneció en debate en algunas regiones hasta el cuarto siglo. El principio detrás de la canonización era el origen apostólico: un libro era Escritura si fue escrito por un apóstol o por alguien que trabajaba bajo autoridad apostólica directa, y si la iglesia en todas partes lo había recibido. La iglesia no creó el canon. La iglesia reconoció el canon. Para cuando Atanasio publicara su famosa Carta Festal del 367 enumerando los veintisiete libros del Nuevo Testamento completos, estaba en gran parte confirmando lo que la mayoría de los cristianos ya sabían.

blocks.en: The unit closes with one quiet observation. Three centuries after Pentecost, the church had survived ten major waves of persecution, defeated three devastating heresies, watched her foundational text get collected, and produced an unbroken chain of teachers from the apostle John to Polycarp to Irenaeus to the verge of Constantine. She had no cathedrals. She had no political power. She had no wealth. She had only the Word, the Spirit, and a remarkable willingness to die. And she was about to win.
blocks.es_reference: La unidad cierra con una observación tranquila. Tres siglos después de Pentecostés, la iglesia había sobrevivido diez olas mayores de persecución, derrotado tres herejías devastadoras, visto su texto fundacional recopilarse, y producido una cadena ininterrumpida de maestros desde el apóstol Juan a Policarpo a Ireneo hasta el borde de Constantino. No tenía catedrales. No tenía poder político. No tenía riqueza. Solo tenía la Palabra, el Espíritu, y una notable disposición a morir. Y estaba a punto de ganar.

blocks.en: Why This Matters for Ministry Today
blocks.es_reference: Por qué esto importa para el ministerio hoy

blocks.en: Three pastoral applications drop out of this period and never go out of date.
blocks.es_reference: Tres aplicaciones pastorales caen de este período y nunca pasan de moda.

blocks.en: First, heresies recycle. Every "new" theological movement that walks through your church door has a second-century ancestor. Modern Gnosticism dresses up as "spirituality" without doctrine, the secret-knowledge feeling without the discipline of the body. Modern Marcionism dresses up as a Jesus stripped of His Old Testament context, a New Testament love without an Old Testament holiness. Modern Montanism dresses up as a continuing revelation that effectively replaces the Bible with the latest prophet. The pastor who knows the second century recognizes the patterns and does not panic. He has seen this before. Irenaeus answered it. He can too.
blocks.es_reference: Primero, las herejías se reciclan. Cada movimiento teológico «nuevo» que cruza la puerta de su iglesia tiene un antepasado del segundo siglo. El gnosticismo moderno se viste como «espiritualidad» sin doctrina, el sentimiento de conocimiento secreto sin la disciplina del cuerpo. El marcionismo moderno se viste como un Jesús despojado de su contexto del Antiguo Testamento, un amor del Nuevo Testamento sin la santidad del Antiguo Testamento. El montanismo moderno se viste como una revelación continua que efectivamente reemplaza la Biblia con el último profeta. El pastor que conoce el segundo siglo reconoce los patrones y no entra en pánico. Ha visto esto antes. Ireneo lo respondió. Él también puede.

blocks.en: Second, persecution is a teacher, not an interruption. The church that has not suffered is the church that has not been tested, and the church that has not been tested does not yet know what she believes. Henrietta Mears used to say that comfort is more dangerous to the church than crisis. Watch the persecuted church in China, in Iran, in Nigeria today. They are not weak. They are stronger than us. The blood that Tertullian called seed is still seed. Plant where blood has been shed, and you will reap a harvest.
blocks.es_reference: Segundo, la persecución es maestra, no interrupción. La iglesia que no ha sufrido es la iglesia que no ha sido probada, y la iglesia que no ha sido probada aún no sabe lo que cree. Henrietta Mears solía decir que la comodidad es más peligrosa para la iglesia que la crisis. Mire a la iglesia perseguida en China, en Irán, en Nigeria hoy. No son débiles. Son más fuertes que nosotros. La sangre que Tertuliano llamó semilla sigue siendo semilla. Plante donde se ha derramado sangre, y cosechará una cosecha.

blocks.en: Third, the chain of teachers matters. You do not stand in your pulpit alone. You stand in a line that runs from Christ to the apostles, from the apostles to Polycarp, from Polycarp to Irenaeus, from Irenaeus through Augustine to Luther to Spurgeon to whoever taught you. That chain is your authority, and it is also your accountability. When you teach, teach what you received. When you receive a student, hand him what you have. "Commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also." Paul wrote that to Timothy in the first century. He could have written it to you this morning.
blocks.es_reference: Tercero, la cadena de maestros importa. Usted no se para solo en su púlpito. Se para en una línea que corre de Cristo a los apóstoles, de los apóstoles a Policarpo, de Policarpo a Ireneo, de Ireneo a través de Agustín a Lutero a Spurgeon a quienquiera le enseñó a usted. Esa cadena es su autoridad, y también su responsabilidad. Cuando enseñe, enseñe lo que recibió. Cuando reciba a un estudiante, entréguele lo que tiene. «Esto encarga a hombres fieles que sean idóneos para enseñar también a otros». Pablo escribió eso a Timoteo en el primer siglo. Pudo haberlo escrito a usted esta mañana.

blocks.en: Closing: The Eve of Constantine
blocks.es_reference: Cierre: La víspera de Constantino

blocks.en: By 311, the Emperor Galerius, dying in agony of an unspecified disease, signed an edict ending the Great Persecution. By 312, Constantine had won the Battle of the Milvian Bridge under what he understood to be the cross of Christ. By 313, Constantine and Licinius had issued the Edict of Milan granting full freedom of worship to Christians. The age of persecution was over. The age of imperial favor had begun.
blocks.es_reference: Para el 311, el Emperador Galerio, muriendo en agonía de una enfermedad no especificada, firmó un edicto que ponía fin a la Gran Persecución. Para el 312, Constantino había ganado la Batalla del Puente Milvio bajo lo que él entendió como la cruz de Cristo. Para el 313, Constantino y Licinio habían emitido el Edicto de Milán otorgando plena libertad de adoración a los cristianos. La era de la persecución había terminado. La era del favor imperial había comenzado.

blocks.en: The church that emerged from those two and a half centuries was a different church than the church that had entered them. She had her canon. She had her creeds in embryonic form. She had her chain of teachers. She had her catalog of heresies and the orthodox answers to them. She had her martyrs, whose stories would feed her memory for centuries. She had Cyprian's wisdom on how to handle the lapsi. She had Tertullian's vocabulary for the Trinity. She had Irenaeus's argument from apostolic succession. And she had a strange new problem coming her way: she was about to be liked. Welcome to Unit 3, which opens with Constantine and the Edict of Milan, walks through the Arian controversy and the great ecumenical councils, and arrives at the second great century of preaching: Chrysostom, the Cappadocians, Ambrose, and a North African bishop's son named Augustine.
blocks.es_reference: La iglesia que emergió de esos dos siglos y medio era una iglesia diferente de la que había entrado en ellos. Tenía su canon. Tenía sus credos en forma embrionaria. Tenía su cadena de maestros. Tenía su catálogo de herejías y las respuestas ortodoxas a ellas. Tenía sus mártires, cuyas historias alimentarían su memoria por siglos. Tenía la sabiduría de Cipriano sobre cómo manejar a los lapsi. Tenía el vocabulario de Tertuliano para la Trinidad. Tenía el argumento de Ireneo desde la sucesión apostólica. Y tenía un problema nuevo y extraño viniendo en su camino: estaba a punto de ser apreciada. Bienvenido a la Unidad 3, que abre con Constantino y el Edicto de Milán, recorre la controversia arriana y los grandes concilios ecuménicos, y llega al segundo gran siglo de predicación: Crisóstomo, los Capadocios, Ambrosio, y el hijo de un obispo norteafricano llamado Agustín.

mc.stem: Who were the Apostolic Fathers?
options: Leaders of Christianity after the Apostles, who were reputed to have known the Apostles and who produced highly valued writings
2nd & 3rd Century Christian scholars who produced comprehensive theological explanations
Intellectual Christians who defended the Church against false charges
The Apostles whom Jesus had trained to lead the Church
mc.why: The Apostolic Fathers were leaders of the late 1st and early 2nd centuries who had personally known or been directly influenced by the apostles. Their writings (like 1 Clement, the letters of Ignatius, the writings of Polycarp, the Didache) bridge the New Testament and later theology.

mc.stem: Who were the Christian Apologists?
options: 2nd & 3rd Century Christian scholars who began to produce more comprehensive theological explanations and defended the Church before pagan culture
Leaders who had known the Apostles and produced highly valued writings
Christians who apologized for the persecutions
The Apostles whom Jesus had trained to lead the Church
mc.why: The Apologists were intellectually trained Christians who defended the faith before pagan emperors and elites. Justin Martyr, Tertullian, and Irenaeus are the major figures. They produced theological explanations that countered both pagan slander and emerging heresy.

mc.stem: Who started the first non-Jewish persecution of Christians, and why?
options: Pontius Pilate, to quell violence after Jesus was crucified
The Emperor Decius, because he wanted to suppress Christianity and revive the old gods
The idol-makers and pagan worshippers of Ephesus
The Emperor Nero, to deflect blame for the burning of Rome
mc.why: Nero blamed Christians for the AD 64 fire of Rome to deflect blame from himself. Tacitus records that he had Christians wrapped in animal skins and torn by dogs, crucified, or burned to light his garden parties. Peter and Paul almost certainly died in this Neronian persecution.

mc.stem: Why did Roman citizens generally dislike Christians and their religion? (Pick the most complete answer.)
options: Christians refused emperor worship, were rumored to commit incest at love feasts and cannibalism at the Eucharist, and were thought to anger the Roman gods
Christians had too much political power
Christians charged too much for baptism
Christians spoke only in Greek
mc.why: Christians were called 'atheists' for refusing the gods, 'incestuous' because of misunderstood love feasts, 'cannibals' because of misunderstood Eucharist language, and were blamed when the gods seemed angry. All four reasons appear in the TH1 scope.

mc.stem: What is the definition of 'heresy'?
options: A formal denial or doubt of a core doctrine of the Christian faith
Claiming to believe the Christian faith but not living according to Christ's instructions
Being unwilling to make a commitment to the Christian faith
Worshipping false gods or idols
mc.why: Heresy is the formal denial of a core doctrine of the faith — not honest disagreement on minor matters, but the rejection or fundamental distortion of something the church has always believed. The Greek root means 'choice' — the choice to pick a piece of truth and exalt it above the whole.

mc.stem: Why did a number of Christian heresies arise in the 2nd Century?
options: Aggressive proselytizing by Roman pagans confused Christians
It was after the death of the apostles but before the New Testament canon was formed and theology had been clearly set
Persian invasions brought Eastern ideas
Conflicts between Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy caused confusion
mc.why: The 2nd century was the perfect window for heresy: apostles dead so first-hand correction was impossible, NT canon not yet collected so disputes were harder to settle, theology not yet articulated so any clever new framework could find an audience.

mc.stem: What was the heresy of Gnosticism?
options: The belief that Gentiles had to be circumcised to become Christians
The belief that the physical world was evil & the spiritual world good, and that secret mystical knowledge was the key to salvation
The belief that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with the Father
A prophetic movement claiming new ecstatic revelations from the Holy Spirit
mc.why: Gnosticism taught radical dualism: spirit good, matter evil. Salvation came through secret 'gnosis' — knowledge — that freed the divine spark from the material body. Most Gnostics were also Docetists who said Christ only seemed to have a body, undermining incarnation, creation, and bodily resurrection.

mc.stem: What was the heresy of Montanism?
options: The belief that Gentiles had to be circumcised to become Christians
The belief that the physical world was evil and salvation was through secret knowledge
The belief that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with the Father
A prophetic movement claiming new and ecstatic revelations from the Holy Spirit that superseded all else
mc.why: Montanism (the 'New Prophecy') taught that the Spirit was speaking new revelations through Montanus and his prophetesses Priscilla and Maximilla, effectively superseding the apostolic deposit just as the New Testament canon was being collected.

mc.stem: What was the heresy of Marcionism?
options: The belief that the physical world was evil and salvation was through secret knowledge
The rejection of the entire Old Testament and most of the New Testament, keeping only an edited Luke and ten Pauline letters
The belief that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with the Father
A prophetic movement claiming new ecstatic revelations
mc.why: Marcion of Sinope (c. 140) rejected the OT entirely, claiming the OT God of judgment was different from Jesus's Father. He kept an edited Luke and ten edited Pauline letters as his canon. The church excommunicated him in 144, but his heretical canon forced the orthodox church to start defining its own canon.

mc.stem: What is meant by the 'Biblical Canon'?
options: The Christian legal system created by the Imperial Church after Constantine
The books Christians consider divinely inspired and rightly included as part of the Christian Bible
The yardstick by which Christians evaluate non-believers
The books of the Apocrypha accepted by Roman Catholics
mc.why: The biblical canon is the collection of books recognized as divinely inspired Scripture. The principle is apostolic origin: a book was Scripture if written by an apostle or under direct apostolic authority, and if the church everywhere had received it. The church did not create the canon; she recognized it.

mc.stem: How did the heretic Marcion influence development of the New Testament canon?
options: By insisting only on John's Gospel as authoritative
By rejecting all of Paul's letters
By proposing his own heretical canon, he forced the orthodox Church to start defining its own canon publicly
By insisting only the Old Testament was canonical
mc.why: Marcion's heretical canon of 144 (edited Luke + ten edited Pauline letters, OT rejected) was the first published Christian canon. The orthodox church responded with its own list. The Muratorian Fragment of c. 170 lists most of the books we now have. Marcion's heresy accelerated the canonization process.

mc.stem: Who were the 'confessors' and why were they important?
options: Jews persecuted in Jerusalem who confessed Jesus as Messiah
Those willing to confess belief in old Roman gods to escape persecution
Authors of the Nicene Creed
Christians who withstood torture and persecution under Decius and Valerian without recanting, and so were revered as spiritual leaders
mc.why: The confessors refused the libellus, were tortured, but survived without recanting. They became living relics of the church's faithfulness, revered as spiritual authorities for the rest of their lives — distinct from the martyrs (who died) and the lapsi (who gave in).

mc.stem: What unique problem did the Church have to face after the persecutions of Decius and Valerian?
options: A complicated mix of those who gave in, fled, falsified documents, and withstood torture forced the Church to figure out how to deal with these different groups
So many martyrs that providing decent burials was impossible
Persecution led to too many sympathy conversions
The Church in Asia Minor was completely destroyed
mc.why: After Decius's libellus system, the church had four groups: martyrs (died), confessors (tortured but survived), fugitives (fled), and lapsi (gave in). The lapsi further split into sacrificati, thurificati, and libellatici. Cyprian of Carthage led the moderate path: readmit the lapsi after public penance.

mc.stem: What is meant by Apostolic Succession?
options: The process by which other leaders were appointed to replace the Apostles after the last (John) died around 100 AD
The policy whereby each Apostle chose his own successor in ministry
The idea of an unbroken ordination chain from the Apostles down to all Christian ministers, so every minister could trace ordination back to an Apostle
The fundamental theological changes implemented after the apostles died
mc.why: Apostolic succession is the idea of an unbroken ordination chain from the apostles to current bishops. Irenaeus used this argument powerfully against the Gnostics: the orthodox church can trace its teachers back to the apostles in a verifiable chain (Polycarp → John, Irenaeus → Polycarp), while heretics cannot.

mc.stem: Why was Apostolic Succession important to the Early Church?
options: It guaranteed the Church would have no heresy
It was thought that if Christian ordination went back unbroken to an Apostle, there was a greater likelihood of correct teaching and spiritual authority
It allowed bishops to control who served in ministry
It helped identify and root out false doctrine completely
mc.why: Apostolic succession was a safeguard against heresy. The argument was that legitimate Christian teaching travels in a verifiable chain from Christ to the apostles to their disciples to the present. The Gnostics could not show such a chain; the orthodox church could. The chain mattered because the message mattered.

mc.stem: Why did the Church around the end of the 2nd Century start having predominantly male leadership?
options: Women proved unable to withstand the demands of ministry
Women decided they wanted nothing to do with the political shenanigans in the Church
Some pre-Christian pagan cults and 2nd-century heresies — notably Gnosticism and Montanism — had women in their leadership, and the orthodox church recoiled
It was finally realized that Jesus and the Twelve Apostles were all men
mc.why: As Priscilla and Maximilla rose to prominence as Montanist prophetesses (and similar patterns appeared in Gnostic groups), the orthodox church recoiled from women in similar visible roles. The first-century pattern of weaving women's gifts into the church's life freely became more cautious in the late 2nd century — a cost of heresy that often goes uncounted.

mc.stem: Polycarp of Smyrna was a disciple of which apostle?
options: Peter
Paul
John
James
mc.why: Polycarp was a disciple of the apostle John. This makes the chain remarkable: John walked with Jesus, taught Polycarp, who taught Irenaeus, who taught the next generation. Two handshakes from Christ.

mc.stem: What famous words did Polycarp say when ordered to deny Christ at age 86?
options: "I am the resurrection and the life"
"Into Your hands I commit my spirit"
"Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do"
"Eighty and six years have I served Him, and He has done me no wrong. How can I blaspheme my King who saved me?"
mc.why: Polycarp's response to the proconsul, recorded in the Martyrdom of Polycarp around AD 155, became the model Christian martyr speech for centuries. Eighty-six years of service, no wrong from his King — therefore no possibility of blasphemy.

mc.stem: Which Apologist coined the Latin word 'Trinity' (trinitas) and famously said the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church?
options: Justin Martyr
Clement of Rome
Irenaeus
Tertullian
mc.why: Tertullian (c. 160–220) was a North African lawyer who gave Western theology its early Latin vocabulary. He coined 'trinitas' (Trinity), defended the faith against Marcion in five volumes, and wrote the famous line: 'The blood of the Christians is seed.'

mc.stem: Which Roman emperor's persecution (250–251) was the first empire-wide demand that every citizen offer sacrifice and obtain a libellus certificate?
options: Nero
Trajan
Decius
Diocletian
mc.why: Decius issued the first empire-wide persecution in 250–251, demanding universal sacrifice with a libellus certificate proving compliance. The libellus system was administrative and devastating, leaving a paper trail that haunted the church and creating the lapsi crisis the church had to sort out afterward.
